complexity_matrix.operation: BFS or DFS traversal, adjacency list
complexity_matrix.notes: Each vertex enqueued once, each edge examined once. Tight against the traversal lower bound.
Same traversal bound. Reports failure when no zero-in-degree vertex remains, which is the cycle certificate.

complexity_matrix.operation: Topological sort on a cyclic graph
complexity_matrix.notes: Terminates with the no-order result rather than looping, because the in-degree argument proves a cycle exists.

complexity_matrix.operation: Dijkstra with a binary heap, non-negative weights
complexity_matrix.notes: V extractions at O(log V) plus E relaxations at O(log V). Requires non-negative weights; unsound otherwise.

complexity_matrix.operation: Dijkstra with an array priority queue (dense graphs)
complexity_matrix.notes: Linear scan to select the minimum. Wins when E is a constant fraction of V^2, loses badly when sparse.

complexity_matrix.operation: Dijkstra on a graph containing a negative edge
complexity_matrix.notes: Returns a wrong answer, not merely a slow one. The invariant that an extracted distance is final fails outright.
V-1 passes over all E edges. The extra factor over Dijkstra is the price of tolerating negative weights.
A V-th pass that still improves a distance proves a negative cycle, and the shortest-path problem is undefined rather than hard.
Best known unconditional all-pairs bound. O(V) per source.

complexity_matrix.operation: Union-find merge with path compression and union by rank
complexity_matrix.notes: Effectively constant amortised; alpha(n) is below 5 for any n that fits in memory. Using only one optimisation loses the bound.
Sort the edges, then V-1 union-find queries. Suits sparse graphs and edge-list input.
Maintains a key per vertex and extracts the minimum. Suits dense adjacency-matrix graphs.

complexity_matrix.operation: BFS distance used where weighted distance is required
complexity_matrix.notes: Returns the fewest-hops path, not the cheapest one. Correct only when all weights are equal.

correctness_argument.claim: Topological sort is correct because a vertex is emitted only at in-degree zero, so every predecessor precedes it, and it detects a cycle exactly when no zero-in-degree vertex remains. Dijkstra is correct because a cheaper path would pass through a not-yet-extracted vertex with a smaller tentative distance, contradicting the extraction order; that argument needs non-negative weights, and with them failing the algorithm returns wrong values.

cost_derivations.claim: Traversal-based algorithms are Theta(V+E) because each vertex is enqueued once and each edge examined once, matching the traversal lower bound. Dijkstra is O((V+E) log V) with a heap and O(V^2) with an array, and Bellman-Ford is Theta(VE) because V-1 passes suffice for paths visiting at most V vertices.
cost_derivations.detail: Union-find reaches O(alpha(n)) amortised only when both path compression and union by rank are used.

limits.claim: Conditionally on the negative-weight triangle hypothesis, no combinatorial algorithm improves O(VE) negative-weight shortest path below O(E^(3-epsilon)), and Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3) is the best known unconditional all-pairs bound. Negative cycles make the problem undefined rather than merely hard. Directed reachability has no O(V+E) sequential algorithm, so a symmetric algorithm for the directed case is a real limitation rather than a shortcut.
